## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials in this search yet. Before this search, only one network family scored above 0: the one with the multi-layout legal-action mask in the input and layout-summed per-type output maps. It reached 0.22 dev in one world, on both recipes tried. Every other trial scored exactly 0, in every world. The likely cause of the uniform zeros is that the world's action indexing does not match the observation grid, so a layout-tied convolutional head cannot learn. Recipe changes alone never helped, so this first round only tests networks, all kept at about the starting compute (r≤1) so they keep the full sample budget. Candidate 1 rebuilds the proven 4-layout family with the default recipe. Candidate 2 widens the hedge to all 8 dihedral layouts, for a world that may be rotated. Candidate 3 adds global context to the 4-layout family. Late training success of 0 would refute the alignment idea for a candidate. Since the starting net's 2 seeds both scored 0.000, any nonzero result is real signal.

### Round 2
All 3 round-1 trials scored exactly 0, with late training success also 0. So did the starting net. The 8-layout dihedral hedge already covered every flip and transpose of the board with brick type as the outermost index, so this world's mismatch is probably not a pure board rotation or flip. A 1x1 stem should learn to reorder the observation channels, and per-type output maps should learn to reorder the brick types, so neither is likely the cause. A board-level mismatch between observation and actions acts the same as a mismatch in action layout. The likely remaining causes are a different place for the brick type in the action index (innermost or middle instead of outermost), or DONE sitting at index 0 so that every placement index is shifted by one. Small anchor shifts should be learnable by the 3x3 receptive field. This round tests broader layout hedges: 24 layouts (every axis order with every flip), then the same plus a DONE-first offset, and that offset version again with a recipe that collects more samples. Nonzero training success is the first real signal.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0, with 0 late training success on every seed. They tried mask-layout hedges with 4, 8, 24 and 48 layouts, global context, and a recipe that gave more samples. That clears action-layout mismatch as this world's problem: the hedges include the as-given layout, so if a layout were the only problem one of them would have found it. That leaves two likely causes. Either the network cannot compute the landing layer and footprint logic, or the world differs in a way the hedges never touched, such as the brick anchor corner, the footprint orientation, or how the observation channels are grouped by layer. The plan is to switch families. The new head is shared across layers: it scores each placement at each layer by pooling over the brick's footprint, then takes a logsumexp over the layers. The input to each layer is built to cover both grouped and interleaved channel orderings. One candidate also hedges the anchor corner and footprint orientation. Another trains the same network on more samples. The first signal to look for is any training success above 0.

### Round 4
All 9 trials and the starting network scored exactly 0, both on dev and on late training success, on both seeds. The trials were mask/action layout hedges (4, 8, 24 and 48 layouts), per-layer footprint heads, an anchor/orientation hedge, and runs with more samples. So the mismatch in this world is probably not in how actions are indexed. Every trial so far assumed the observation tensor is laid out as described ([C, Y, X]). If the world stores it differently (for example in [Y, X, C] memory order, or with Y and X swapped), each channel would hold scrambled positions. A 1x1 stem and small convolutions cannot undo that, which would explain why every network fails the same way. Undoing a reshape before the first learned layer is allowed. So this round hedges the observation layout: all 6 orderings of the (C, Y, X) axes are fed in as channels, combined with the only family that has ever scored above 0. The three candidates differ in output hedge and recipe.
